positions.text: Hasan, Brunie, and Bertino independently specify the identity-binding mechanism behind Kaal's claim. Their survey distinguishes pseudonym-bound reputation, which a participant can abandon by re-entering under a fresh pseudonym, from identity-bound reputation that survives pseudonym changes; in the surveyed BPRF design, PKI recognition reassigns prior reputation after exit and re-entry and thereby resists Sybil and whitewashing attacks. This supports persistence as a defense against costless history shedding, while qualifying Kaal's design: the surveyed mechanism is human- and PKI-bound and does not establish per-capability agent tags, non-transferability between tags, or the substrate's wider incentives.

sourceEvidencePassages.text: A privacy-preserving reputation system can be either pseudonym-bound or identity-bound. In a pseudonym-bound system, the reputation of the ratee is associated with her pseudonym. If she changes or creates a new pseudonym, then she looses her reputation. The use of pseudonyms has the drawback that the reputation is not transferable between a ratee’s multiple pseudonyms. An additional major drawback is that a dishonest ratee can drop a pseudonym with bad reputation and re-enter the system with a new pseudonym and a fresh reputation. This common attack against pseudonym-bound systems is known as whitewashing.

On the other hand, in an identity-bound system, the reputation of a ratee is bound to her real identity. Even if she changes pseudonyms, she maintains her reputation. This is often made possible by verifying the true identity of a ratee before issuing a new pseudonym.

Reputation is identity-bound because users are authenticated using a PKI. If they exit and re-enter the system, they can be recognized and re-assigned their existing reputation. This mechanism provides strong resistance against Sybil attacks and whitewashing.
